# Spotify Project

Understanding what makes a song popular has always been a topic of interest for artists, producers, and researchers. With the increasing availability of music data from platforms like Spotify and Billboard, we now have the opportunity to analyze musical trends over time using quantitative methods.

In this project, we aim to investigate whether it is possible to predict a song’s popularity based on its audio features. We begin with a broad historical analysis spanning from 1956 to today, then narrow our focus to the last 25 years, a period we believe better reflects modern listening habits and production styles.

Through data preprocessing, feature engineering, and statistical analysis, we build and evaluate models to forecast not only immediate success but also a song’s long-term presence in the charts. Our goal is to better understand the relationship between music characteristics and commercial success, and to explore how this relationship has evolved over time.

**Abstract**: This project explores the evolution of music from 1956 to the present, with a focus on predicting song popularity based on audio features. After an initial global analysis, we restrict our attention to the last 25 years to better reflect contemporary musical trends and production standards. Using statistical analysis and machine learning models, we assess the relationship between audio characteristics and a song's chart success. We also conduct hypothesis testing to evaluate how changes in music over time impact our findings. Finally, we propose two models aimed at predicting not only a song's immediate popularity, but also its long-term staying power in the charts.

link to the **dataset**: [jonhthgeek-DataSetSpotify](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2021/2021-09-14/readme.md)

```r
# count NaN for each column
count_na_per_column <- function(data) {
  sapply(data, function(col) sum(is.na(col)))}

count_na_per_column_df <- function(data) {
  na_counts <- sapply(data, function(col) sum(is.na(col)))
  na_counts_df <- data.frame(
    feature = names(na_counts),
    na_count = na_counts
  )
  na_counts_df %>% arrange(desc(na_count))
}

# extract first genre for the spotify genre
extract_first_genre <- function(df, genre_column = "spotify_genre") {
  # check if column exists
  if (!genre_column %in% colnames(df)) {
    stop(paste("La colonna", genre_column, "non esiste nel dataframe"))
  }
  
  # removes useless not required characters
  df[[genre_column]] <- gsub("\\[|\\]|'", "", df[[genre_column]])
  
  # create a list, with div = ,
  genre_list <- strsplit(df[[genre_column]], split = ",")
  
  # extract only the first genre for each line or rename "others"
  df$first_genre <- sapply(genre_list, function(x) {
    x <- trimws(x)  # remove blanks
    if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x[1]) || x[1] == "") {
      return("others")
    } else {
      return(x[1])
    }
  })
  
  # convert to categorical value
  df$first_genre <- as.factor(df$first_genre)
  
  # output
  return(df)
}

# process and encode the genre column
process_and_encode_genre <- function(df, genre_column = "first_genre", top_n = 15) {
  # check if column exists
  if (!genre_column %in% colnames(df)) {
    stop(paste("La colonna", genre_column, "non esiste nel dataframe"))
  }
  
  # count the frequency
  genre_counts <- table(df[[genre_column]])
  
  # put them in decrescent order
  genre_counts_sorted <- sort(genre_counts, decreasing = TRUE)
  
  # take top N genres
  top_genres <- names(genre_counts_sorted)[1:min(top_n, length(genre_counts_sorted))]
  
  # rename not in top N into 'others'
  df[[genre_column]] <- ifelse(
    df[[genre_column]] %in% top_genres,
    df[[genre_column]],
    "others"
  )
  
  # convert
  df[[genre_column]] <- as.factor(df[[genre_column]])
  
  # remove original column
  if ("spotify_genre" %in% colnames(df)) {
    df <- subset(df, select = -c(spotify_genre))
  }
  
  # create dummy variables (one-hot encoding)
  dummy <- dummyVars(paste("~", genre_column), data = df)
  dummy_df <- data.frame(predict(dummy, newdata = df))
  
  final_df <- bind_cols(
    df %>% select(-all_of(genre_column)),
    dummy_df
  )
  
  # output
  return(final_df)
}

# encode popularity column
encode_spotify_popularity <- function(df, column = "spotify_track_popularity") {
  # check if column exists
  if (!column %in% colnames(df)) {
    stop(paste("La colonna", column, "non esiste nel dataframe"))
  }
  
  categorize_popularity <- function(x) {
    if (is.na(x)) return(NA)
    if (x <= 25) {
      return("low")
    } else if (x <= 50) {
      return("medium")
    } else if (x <= 75) {
      return("high")
    } else if (x <= 100) {
      return("very high")
    } else {
      return(NA)  # out of range
    }
  }
  
  df[[column]] <- sapply(df[[column]], categorize_popularity)
  
  # convert in ordered factor
  df[[column]] <- factor(df[[column]], 
                         levels = c("low", "medium", "high", "very high"), 
                         ordered = TRUE)
  
  # output
  return(df)
}

# plots the confusion matrix
plot_conf_matrix <- function(conf_matrix_object, title = "Confusion Matrix") {
  
  # converts confusion matrix into dataframe
  cm_df <- as.data.frame(conf_matrix_object$table)
  
  # find columns names (Truth, Prediction, Freq)
  colnames(cm_df) <- tolower(colnames(cm_df)) # rende tutto minuscolo
  
  # rename them
  names(cm_df)[names(cm_df) %in% c("reference", "truth")] <- "Actual"
  names(cm_df)[names(cm_df) == "prediction"] <- "Predicted"
  names(cm_df)[names(cm_df) %in% c("freq", "n")] <- "Freq"
  
  # plot
  p <- ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5, color = "black") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = title,
         x = "Predicted Class",
         y = "Actual Class",
         fill = "Count") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
  
  return(p)
}
```

<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

The dataset consists of 298,117 rows and 22 columns. Each row represents a weekly chart appearance of a song, not a unique song itself — which means the same song may appear multiple times with different `week_id` values.

The columns contain a wide range of information:

- **Chart metadata**: such as `week_id`, `week_position`, `previous_week_position`, `peak_position`, and `weeks_on_chart`.
- **Song information**: including `performer`, `song_id`, and `spotify_genre`.
- **Spotify audio features**: such as `danceability`, `energy`, `acousticness`, `valence`, and `tempo`, which describe the musical properties of the tracks.
- **Additional metadata**: including `spotify_track_duration_ms`, `key`, `mode`, `speechiness`, `instrumentalness`, `liveness`, and `time_signature`.
- **Popularity**: The column `spotify_track_popularity` provides Spotify's internal popularity score, which can be useful as a target or benchmark in predictive tasks.

It is also important to note that some values are missing (`NA`), especially in Spotify-related fields, likely due to older songs not being available or fully processed on Spotify.



<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin eyJkYXRhIjoiXG48IS0tIHJuYi1zb3VyY2UtYmVnaW4gZXlKa1lYUmhJam9pWUdCZ2NseHVjM1Z0YldGeWVTaG1kV3hzWDJSaGRHRXBYRzVnWUdBaWZRPT0gLS0+XG5cbmBgYHJcbnN1bW1hcnkoZnVsbF9kYXRhKVxuYGBgXG5cbjwhLS0gcm5iLXNvdXJjZS1lbmQgLS0+XG4ifQ== -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin eyJkYXRhIjoiYGBgclxuc3VtbWFyeShmdWxsX2RhdGEpXG5gYGAifQ== -->

```r
summary(full_data)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

This summary provides descriptive statistics for the dataset's variables.

- **Chart-related variables** such as `week_position`, `previous_week_position`, and `peak_position` range from 1 to 100, with a fairly uniform median around 46–47. The number of weeks a song remains on the chart (`weeks_on_chart`) ranges from 2 to 87, with a median of 8 weeks.

- **Track duration** (`spotify_track_duration_ms`) varies significantly, with a median of about 3.75 minutes (225,173 ms) and some outliers over 50 minutes, suggesting the presence of non-standard tracks (e.g., extended versions or errors). Around 13% of entries lack this information (`NA`s).

- **Audio features** (from Spotify) such as `danceability`, `energy`, `valence`, and `tempo` show a wide distribution:
  - `Danceability` and `energy` have median values around 0.62 and 0.65, respectively, indicating moderately upbeat music on average.
  - `Valence` (musical positivity) has a median of 0.62, suggesting a tendency toward emotionally positive tracks.
  - `Tempo` ranges from 0 to over 240 BPM, with a median around 118 BPM, typical of many popular genres.

- **Musical characteristics** such as `key`, `mode`, and `time_signature` confirm that most tracks are in common time (4/4), with keys distributed across the full 0–11 range (representing the 12 semitones).

- **Other audio descriptors**:
  - `Speechiness` and `instrumentalness` are mostly low, which is expected in mainstream songs.
  - `Acousticness` and `liveness` show a broader spread, indicating a mix of electronic and live/acoustic content.

- **Popularity** (`spotify_track_popularity`) ranges from 0 to 100, with a median of 51. This variable could be considered as a potential target for prediction tasks. Like many other Spotify features, it has missing values in about 13% of rows.

Overall, this summary confirms that the dataset is rich and varied, but also highlights the need to address missing values (notably in Spotify-provided fields) before modeling or deeper analysis.


### 2.1 Missing Values

<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin eyJkYXRhIjoiYGBgclxubmFfY291bnRzIDwtIGNvdW50X25hX3Blcl9jb2x1bW5fZGYoZnVsbF9kYXRhKVxucHJpbnQobmFfY291bnRzKVxuYGBgIn0= -->

```r
na_counts <- count_na_per_column_df(full_data)
print(na_counts)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->


The original dataset contained 39,819 missing values in various Spotify-related columns (approximately 13% of the total 298,117 rows).

To address this, we applied the following cleaning strategy:

- For the `previous_week_position` variable, missing values were replaced with `0`, under the assumption that songs entering the chart for the first time do not have a previous position.

- For all other missing values, we removed the corresponding rows using `na.omit()`. This resulted in a cleaned dataset (`full_data_clean`) with **258,298 rows** and **22 columns**, preserving the structure while reducing the potential impact of missing or incomplete data on the analysis.

We considered this data loss acceptable, as the percentage of removed rows was relatively small and unlikely to introduce significant bias.


<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
full_data_clean <- full_data
full_data_clean$previous_week_position[is.na(full_data_clean$previous_week_position)] <- 0 # substitute NaN with 0
full_data_clean <- na.omit(full_data_clean) # remove all NaN

nrow(full_data_clean)
ncol(full_data_clean) 

```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

### 2.2 Distributions

Distribution of numeric data

<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->

```r
numeric_data <- full_data_clean |> select(where(is.numeric))

numeric_data_long <- numeric_data |> pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

# histograms distribution facet
ggplot(numeric_data_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", bins = 25) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +  # 3 columns
  theme_minimal()
#ggsave("0_numeric_histogram_distribution.png", width = 12, height = 16)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

The histogram grid above shows the distribution of key numerical features in the cleaned dataset. Several observations can be made:

- **Audio features** such as `danceability`, `energy`, and `tempo` tend to follow approximately normal or slightly skewed distributions:
  - `Danceability` and `energy` peak around 0.6, suggesting that most songs are rhythmically engaging and energetic.
  - `Tempo` shows a near-normal distribution centered around 120 BPM, which aligns with the typical tempo of pop music.

- `Acousticness`, `instrumentalness`, and `speechiness` are highly right-skewed:
  - Most songs have low values of `acousticness` and `instrumentalness`, indicating a predominance of electronically produced and vocal-heavy tracks.
  - `Speechiness` values are concentrated near 0, suggesting that most songs are musical rather than spoken word (e.g., podcasts or rap with high spoken-word content are rare in the dataset).

- **`Loudness`** follows a left-skewed distribution with a peak around -7 to -10 dB, reflecting the mastering norms in popular music.

- **Chart metrics** (`week_position`, `peak_position`) are heavily skewed toward lower values, meaning that only a small fraction of songs reach top positions.

- **`Weeks_on_chart`** shows that the majority of songs stay on the chart for fewer than 15 weeks, with only a few lasting longer than 30 weeks.

- **Categorical-like features** such as `key`, `mode`, and `time_signature` are shown as numerical:
  - The musical **key** is relatively evenly distributed across the 12 semitones, although some keys (e.g., 0, 5, 7) appear more often.
  - **Mode** is binary and skewed toward major mode (`1`), reflecting the general preference for major-key music in popular songs.
  - Most songs use a **time signature** of 4/4 (`4`), which is expected in mainstream music.

- **Spotify-specific features** like `spotify_track_popularity` show a moderately normal distribution of popularity scores, centered around 50.

Others seems to be all clustered in one bin and need to be explored furthermore.

QQ-plots are used to assess whether a variable follows a normal distribution by comparing observed and theoretical quantiles.
From the plots, it is evident that none of the features are `perfectly normally distributed`. However, some variables such as `week_position`, `previous_week_position`, `peak_position`, `danceability` `energy` show a fairly linear pattern in the central part, suggesting an approximately normal distribution.

Other features (e.g., `acousticness`, `instrumentalness`, `speechiness`, `liveness`) exhibit strong deviations, indicating skewness or the presence of outliers.

To better understand the categorical variables with high cardinality, we visualized the frequency of the top 50 most common values for each feature:

- `Performer`:  
  The distribution shows a relatively balanced frequency across the top 50 performers, with a few artists standing out with over 750 occurrences. This suggests that some performers consistently appear in the charts (possibly due to sustained popularity or multiple hit songs), while the rest have moderate chart presence.

- `Song ID`:  
  Song appearances are fairly uniformly distributed among the top 50 songs, with each appearing between roughly 50 and 100 times. This indicates a fairly even recurrence of popular songs across different weeks, with no single track overwhelmingly dominating the dataset.

- `Spotify Genre`:  
  The genre distribution is more skewed. A few genres (possibly "pop", "dance pop", or "rap") dominate the top frequencies, with one genre exceeding 12,000 entries—suggesting a strong genre concentration in the dataset. The long tail highlights a wide variety of niche genres with fewer appearances.

- `Week ID`:  
  The number of records per week appears relatively consistent with some fluctuations. A slight increase toward the middle of the chart could indicate growing data volume or more tracked songs over time. The presence of a few dips may suggest data irregularities, holidays, or temporary drops in chart activity.



These distributions help us understand the overall composition of the dataset and guide future decisions for modeling and feature engineering.

### 2.4 Outliers


<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
# histograms distribution facet
ggplot(numeric_data_long, aes(x = value, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + 
  theme_minimal()
#ggsave("0_numeric_boxplot_distribution.png", width = 12, height = 16)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->


Through the boxplots of numerical features, we can observe the presence and distribution of outliers.  
Below is a summary of the most significant variables:

- **Many outliers are present in:**
  - `instrumentalness`: all values above zero are marked as outliers. As seen earlier, this is because the vast majority of songs have this value at 0. For this reason, this feature will likely be discarded, as it is not relevant to our analysis.
  - `speechiness`: several values above 0.3 are considered outliers; this indicates tracks with a strong vocal component (e.g., spoken word, rap).
  - `spotify_track_duration_ms`: some tracks have extremely long durations (over 2 million milliseconds, i.e., ~30 minutes), which are anomalies compared to the average song length.
  - `tempo`: some values above 200 BPM are rare and constitute outliers.
  - `weeks_on_chart`: many points above the upper limit suggest a long chart presence for some songs, though they are not necessarily errors.
  - `liveness` and `instrumentalness`: show skewed distributions with some extreme values close to 1.

- **Features with few or no outliers:**
  - `mode` and `key`: these are numerical categorical variables and show compact distributions without real outliers.
  - `valence`, `danceability`, `energy`, and `acousticness`: these have more regular distributions, with few extreme values.

- **Ordinal features (e.g., `peak_position`, `week_position`, `previous_week_position`)**:  
  Outliers correspond to songs that ranked very high (low position numbers) or very low (high positions). These are not errors but actual reflections of chart dynamics.

- Some outliers (e.g., excessively long durations or very high `tempo`) could be data entry errors and should be evaluated individually.
- In other cases, such as `weeks_on_chart` or `speechiness`, outliers reflect real-world behavior (long-lasting hits or spoken tracks).

Depending on the model used, we may:
- keep the outliers if they make sense from a musical or commercial perspective;
- normalize or transform them (e.g., log transformation for `spotify_track_duration_ms`);
- or remove them if they are clearly erroneous or so rare that they distort the results.

# compute correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_data, use = "complete.obs")

# correlation heatmap
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "color", 
         type = "upper", tl.col = "black", 
         #number.cex = 0.7, addCoef.col = "black",

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->


The correlation matrix is a powerful tool, especially relevant when working with models where feature independence is important.  

From the matrix, we can observe that, as expected, the three Billboard-related features — `week_position`, `previous_week_position`, and `peak_position` — are strongly correlated with each other. Additionally, `weeks_on_chart` is also correlated, though less strongly and in a negative direction.

All other features show no significant correlations and can be considered independent. The only mild correlation is between `energy` and `acousticness`, which makes sense as more energetic songs tend to have less acoustic content (e.g., louder sounds, stronger beats).

In conclusion, the only significantly correlated features that may pose a problem are the Billboard-related variables.


## 3. Global Preprocessing
Global preprocessing is a crucial step when working with large, heterogeneous datasets like Billboard rankings and Spotify audio features. The raw data is typically recorded at a weekly level and contains many duplicate song entries across time. Without preprocessing, the dataset would be too granular and redundant for most machine learning models or meaningful statistical analysis.

By aggregating the data at the song level, we:
- **Reduce redundancy**, turning multiple weekly entries into a single representative row per song.
- **Summarize chart performance** (e.g., best, worst, average position), which better captures a song’s commercial success.
- **Enable feature merging** by aligning temporal data with static audio features.
- **Improve model performance** by reducing noise and dimensionality.
- **Prepare for clean, structured input** for clustering, classification, or regression models.

This step ensures that we work with a consistent and compact dataset that better reflects the properties and success of individual songs, rather than noisy week-by-week fluctuations.


### 3.1 Aggregations
In this step, we aggregate the weekly Billboard data at the song level to obtain summary statistics that represent a song's overall chart performance. This helps reduce redundancy and simplifies analysis by transforming time-series data into one record per song.



<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
# new features creation
billboard_summary <- billboard %>%
  group_by(song_id) %>%
  summarise(
    min_position = min(week_position),
    max_position = max(week_position),
    avg_position = mean(week_position),
    weeks_in_chart = n_distinct(week_id),
    final_position = last(week_position)
  )

full_data_aggregate <- merge(billboard_summary, audio_features, by = "song_id", all = FALSE)
full_data_aggregate <- full_data_aggregate %>% select(-c(instrumentalness, time_signature))

print(head(full_data_aggregate, 5))

```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(furrr)
set.seed(45)

plan(multisession, workers = 6)

# 1. Split
split <- initial_split(regression_data_encoded_scaled, prop = 0.8)
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

# 2. Recipe
recipe_spec <- recipe(spotify_track_popularity ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE)

# 3. Resampling (non usato direttamente, ma mantenuto)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5)

# 4. Modelli con parametri fissi
models <- list(
  rf = rand_forest(mtry = 5, trees = 500) %>%
    set_engine("randomForest") %>% set_mode("regression"),

  xgb = boost_tree(trees = 1000, tree_depth = 6, learn_rate = 0.1) %>%
    set_engine("xgboost") %>% set_mode("regression"),

  knn = nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 7) %>%
    set_engine("kknn") %>% set_mode("regression")
)

# 5. Workflow per ciascun modello
workflows_list <- purrr::imap(models, function(model, name) {
  workflow() %>%
    add_model(model) %>%
    add_recipe(recipe_spec)
})

# 6. Fit parallelo
final_models <- furrr::future_map(workflows_list, function(wf) {
  library(tidymodels)  # necessario dentro il worker
  fit(wf, data = train_data)
})

# 7. Predizione + metriche parallele
results <- furrr::future_map(final_models, ~ {
  predict(.x, test_data) %>%
    bind_cols(test_data) %>%
    metrics(truth = spotify_track_popularity, estimate = .pred)
})

# 8. Riassunto risultati
results_df <- bind_rows(results, .id = "model") %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  arrange(.estimate)

print(results_df)

# Torna a sequenziale
plan(sequential)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->



<!-- rnb-text-end -->

As you can clearly state from the Regressions above, the model is not predicting well the popularity of the song. All three of the model used in this task have a low performance. The lowest RMSE comes from the Random Forest regressor with a value of 16.8 and is quite high. If the true value of the popularity of one song is 50 that means that our model could predict a value that goes from 31.2 to 66.8 and this is not precise enough for us. Is there a way to improve the model performances reducing the RMSE?

First let's try to understand wich features are the most imporant for our model.

features importance

```r
# VIP plot list
vip_plots <- list()

# Random Forest
rf_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_models$rf)
if (inherits(rf_fit$fit, "randomForest")) {
  vip_plots$rf <- vip(rf_fit$fit, num_features = 15) + ggtitle("Random Forest")
}

# XGBoost
xgb_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_models$xgb)
if (inherits(xgb_fit$fit, "xgb.Booster")) {
  vip_plots$xgb <- vip(xgb_fit$fit, num_features = 15) + ggtitle("XGBoost")
}

# visualize plots
library(patchwork)

# show them
if (length(vip_plots) == 2) {
  vip_plots$rf + vip_plots$xgb
} else {
  # if only one is possible
  vip_plots[[1]]
}
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

The models have identified the same set of features as the most important. Loudness consistently ranks first, followed by the duration of the track in second place. Beyond these common top features, the models prioritize the remaining variables in slightly different orders.

One potential strategy to improve our model's performance is to bin the target variable, popularity, and evaluate whether this transformation enhances predictive accuracy.

We have chosen to divide the popularity scores into four bins, each spanning 25 points, and label them as follows:

- **Low**
- **Medium**
- **High**
- **Very High**

```r
set.seed(45)
library(tidymodels)
library(furrr)

plan(multisession, workers = 6)

# 1. Split
split <- initial_split(regression_data_after, prop = 0.8)
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

# 2. Recipe
recipe_spec <- recipe(spotify_track_popularity ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE)

# 3. Resampling (non usato qui)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5)

# 4. Modelli con parametri fissi
models <- list(
  rf = rand_forest(mtry = 5, trees = 500) %>%
    set_engine("randomForest") %>% set_mode("regression"),

  xgb = boost_tree(trees = 1000, tree_depth = 6, learn_rate = 0.1) %>%
    set_engine("xgboost") %>% set_mode("regression"),

  knn = nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 7) %>%
    set_engine("kknn") %>% set_mode("regression")
)

# 5. Workflows
workflows_list <- purrr::imap(models, function(model, name) {
  workflow() %>%
    add_model(model) %>%
    add_recipe(recipe_spec)
})

# 6. Fit parallelo
final_models <- furrr::future_map(workflows_list, function(wf) {
  library(tidymodels)  # necessario dentro il worker
  fit(wf, data = train_data)
})

# 7. Valuta su test set in parallelo
results <- furrr::future_map(final_models, ~ {
  predict(.x, test_data) %>%
    bind_cols(test_data) %>%
    metrics(truth = spotify_track_popularity, estimate = .pred)
})

# 8. Riassunto RMSE
results_df <- bind_rows(results, .id = "model") %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  arrange(.estimate)

print(results_df)

# (opzionale) chiudi il cluster
plan(sequential)
```

The new models trained exclusively on songs released between 2010 and 2021 are more accurate than the general ones. This is encouraging, as it shows that we can make more reliable predictions for music from the past 10 years or so.

With these new models, the lowest RMSE is now around 10 — a significant improvement compared to previous results. For example, if we aim to predict a popularity score of 50 for a given song, the model would  return a value between 40 and 60. This range is much more acceptable and useful for practical purposes.

While the predictions are still not perfect, they are clearly better than before.

Also here we see that acousticness between 2010 and 2021 is on average higher than in the past years.

In conclusion, we can observe a significant change in various aspects of songs throughout this historical period. The second half of the 20th century was undoubtedly marked by the emergence of many distinct musical styles, and due to this great variety, it becomes very difficult to build a model that can accurately predict the popularity of a song across the entire timespan.  

It makes much more sense to train smaller models on just a specific portion of this period if we aim to obtain more precise predictions.  

It would also be interesting to apply this approach separately to different continents — or even individual countries — in order to more accurately capture the musical preferences of people living in those regions.

}

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->


Based on the QQ plots for the periods before and after 2010, none of the feature distributions appear to be normal. Therefore, to compare the two distributions, we should use the Wilcoxon test.

#### Hypothesis Test

<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
#Doing a wilcox test based on the track_duration of the songs
wilcox.test(
  hypothesis_data_after$spotify_track_duration_min,
  hypothesis_data_before$spotify_track_duration_min,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

#filtering the datasets with only the track_duration feature
loudness_after <- hypothesis_data_after$spotify_track_duration_min
loudness_before <- hypothesis_data_before$spotify_track_duration_min


plot(density(loudness_after), col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "Spotify track duration min Density: After 2010 vs Before 2010", xlab = "duration")
lines(density(loudness_before), col = "red", lwd = 2)

legend("topright", legend = c("After 2010", "Before 2010"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

The p-value from this test is very close to the acceptance of H1 but is just to high for us. This could be due to an unlucky case. Anyway we can see that the duration of the tracks after 2010 are more focused on a single mean just under 4 minutes, while the ones before are a bit more spread out between 2 and 4 minutes. Anyway we dont see much difference in the two distributions.



<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
#Doing a wilcox test based on the energy of the songs
wilcox.test(
  hypothesis_data_after$energy,
  hypothesis_data_before$energy,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

#filtering the datasets with only the energy feature
energy_after <- hypothesis_data_after$energy
energy_before <- hypothesis_data_before$energy


plot(density(energy_after), col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "Energy Density: After 2010 vs Before 2010", xlab = "energy")
lines(density(energy_before), col = "red", lwd = 2)

legend("topright", legend = c("After 2010", "Before 2010"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

As we can see from the two distributions, they are similar, but the results of the Wilcox test says otherwise, the p-value is less than 0.05, meaning that we need to reject the hypothesis test. In other words, even if the distribution seems the same, the energy of the songs after 2010 are not like the ones released before.



<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
#Doing a wilcox test based on the loudness of the songs
wilcox.test(
  hypothesis_data_after$loudness,
  hypothesis_data_before$loudness,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

#filtering the datasets with only the loudness feature
loudness_after <- hypothesis_data_after$loudness
loudness_before <- hypothesis_data_before$loudness


plot(density(loudness_after), col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "Loudness Density: After 2010 vs Before 2010", xlab = "loudness")
lines(density(loudness_before), col = "red", lwd = 2)

legend("topright", legend = c("After 2010", "Before 2010"), col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->



From what we can see above, the two periods have different distributions, even without looking at the wilcox test, that the outcome of it is less than 0.05, ending up with rejecting the null hypothesis. In other words, the loudness of the songs after 2010 are not like the ones released before.

##Future Improovements
After all this considerations we can say that there are many aspects that we have not considered. The Billboard dataset is much more suitable for timeseries analysis but we still do not have the capabilities to do that kind of evaluations. It would be very interesting to try to predict the position of a song in the next future based on his past. Anyway one thing that surely could be added to the dataset used for this project is the year of production of the different songs, this could help us in creating a model that maybe fitted the general period instead of just one snaphsot. This way the model would have an helpful reference on which different "styles" or genres were popular in a particular period.

```r
set.seed(45)
split <- initial_split(head(regression_data_encoded,100), prop = 0.8)
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

# recipe
recipe_spec <- recipe(final_position ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE)

task = 'regression'

# models
models <- list(
  rf = rand_forest(mtry = 5) %>% set_engine("randomForest") %>% set_mode(task),
  xgb = boost_tree(trees = 100, tree_depth = 10) %>% set_engine("xgboost") %>% set_mode(task),
  knn = nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 5) %>% set_engine("kknn") %>% set_mode(task)
)

# workflow
workflows_list <- purrr::map(models, ~ workflow() %>% add_model(.x) %>% add_recipe(recipe_spec))

# train models
fitted_models <- purrr::map(workflows_list, ~ fit(.x, data = train_data))

# evaluation
results <- purrr::map(fitted_models, ~ {
  predict(.x, test_data) %>%
    bind_cols(test_data) %>%
    metrics(truth = final_position, estimate = .pred)
})

# results
results_df <- bind_rows(results, .id = "model")

results_df %>%
  filter(.metric == "rmse") %>%
  arrange(.estimate)

print(results_df)
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->

From the results obtained, we can observe that for the models is difficult to predict the exact position of a particular song in the billboard, with an rmse between 20-27%. Even with an error that high, the random forest keep performing better than the others two. With an error like this, if we would try to predict the position of a song, it will have an error of about +-20 places. This highlights the difficulty of the task.


<!-- rnb-text-end -->


<!-- rnb-chunk-begin -->


<!-- rnb-output-begin  -->


<!-- rnb-source-begin  -->

```r
# VIP plot list
vip_plots <- list()

# Random Forest
rf_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(fitted_models$rf)
if (inherits(rf_fit$fit, "randomForest")) {
  vip_plots$rf <- vip(rf_fit$fit, num_features = 15) + ggtitle("Random Forest - Variable Importance")
}

# XGBoost
xgb_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(fitted_models$xgb)
if (inherits(xgb_fit$fit, "xgb.Booster")) {
  vip_plots$xgb <- vip(xgb_fit$fit, num_features = 15) + ggtitle("XGBoost - Variable Importance")
}

# visualize plots
library(patchwork)

# show them
if (length(vip_plots) == 2) {
  vip_plots$rf + vip_plots$xgb
} else {
  # if only one is possible
  vip_plots[[1]]
}
```

<!-- rnb-source-end -->


<!-- rnb-output-end -->

<!-- rnb-chunk-end -->


<!-- rnb-text-begin -->


From what we can see here for both models, the average, max and min position are the most important features for predicting the position of a song. The importance of features decrease drastically after the first three for the XGboost model, meaning that they are irrelevant for predicting the position of the song.

# Conclusion
In conclusion we can't predict the level of a song with just using the audio feature, because with an RMSE of 16.8, the means predictions could deviate by +-16.8, which is too imprecise for practical use. Same problem with the classification problem, it's too much inaccurate to use it in real world application.

On the other way, we can predict the popularity level of a song if we use both audio features and their recent performance statistics, not perfectly but with an acceptable margin of error.

The songs' features changed over time, like loudness and energy, while just a few didn't change so much, like the track duration.

We tried to develop some models, both for regression and classification, about predicting the position of a song based on the audio features and some positional history records. For the regression model, we end up with a RMSE of 20, making it impossible for real world usage, while the classification model, worked better than we expected, having an accuracy of 90% but with a 50% chanche to classify a song as in top30, while il reality is not.






<!-- rnb-text-end -->
